title: Stacks
definition: A stack is a linear data structure that follows the Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) principle. Elements are added and removed only from one end, called the top.
conceptExplanation: The LIFO principle means the last element pushed onto the stack is the first one to be popped. The two primary operations are push (add to top) and pop (remove from top). Peek/Top returns the top element without removing it.
keyPoints: - LIFO principle - Operations at one end (top) - Push, Pop, Peek operations - Array or linked implementation
importantTerminology: Stack, Top, Push, Pop, Peek, Underflow, Overflow, LIFO
workingPrinciple: Push adds an element to the top of the stack, incrementing the top pointer. Pop removes the top element, decrementing the top pointer. Peek returns the top element without removing it. If push is attempted on a full stack, it causes overflow. If pop is attempted on an empty stack, it causes underflow.
realLifeExample: Browser back button, undo/redo in text editors, function call stack, expression evaluation
dsaExample: Evaluating postfix expressions, converting infix to postfix, checking balanced parentheses
diagram: Stack operations showing push and pop: top -> [50] -> [40] -> [30] (top moves with each operation)
algorithm:
Push Operation:
1. Check if stack is full (overflow)
2. If not, increment top pointer
3. Add element at top position
4. Return success

Pop Operation:
1. Check if stack is empty (underflow)
2. If not, get element at top
3. Decrement top pointer
4. Return removed element

Peek Operation:
1. Check if stack is empty
2. Return element at top position without removing it
pseudocode:
BEGIN
  // Push
  IF stack IS full
    PRINT 'Overflow'
  ELSE
    SET top = top + 1
    SET stack[top] = item
  END IF

  // Pop
  IF stack IS empty
    PRINT 'Underflow'
  ELSE
    SET item = stack[top]
    SET top = top - 1
  END IF

  // Peek
  IF stack IS empty
    PRINT 'Stack is empty'
  ELSE
    PRINT 'Top element:', stack[top]
  END IF
END
complexity: Time: Push O(1), Pop O(1), Peek O(1)\nSpace: O(n) for n elements (capacity limited)
applications: Browser back button, undo/redo functionality, function call stack, expression evaluation, backtracking algorithms
advantages: O(1) push/pop operations, simple implementation, memory efficient (array-based), LIFO order useful for many algorithms
limitations: Fixed size (array-based), limited to LIFO operations only, stack overflow possible
commonMistakes: Confusing push/pop with queue operations (FIFO), not checking for overflow/underflow, using wrong index for peek
importantExamPoints:

Array vs linked implementation differences
Overflow and underflow conditions
Use cases: recursion, expression parsing, backtracking

fiveMarkQuestions.question: Explain stack operations, implementations, and applications.
fiveMarkQuestions.answer:
A stack is a linear data structure following LIFO (Last-In-First-Out) principle. Operations: - Push: Adds element to top. Time: O(1). - Pop: Removes element from top. Time: O(1). - Peek/Top: Returns top element without removal. Time: O(1). - isEmpty: Checks if stack is empty. - isFull: Checks if stack capacity reached.

Array Implementation: Fixed capacity, top index tracks top element, items stored in array. Operations are O(1).
Linked Implementation: Dynamic size, each node contains data and next pointer. Head represents top. No fixed capacity.

Applications: Browser back button (last visited page first), undo/redo in editors, function call stack (each function call pushes return address), evaluating postfix expressions, converting infix to postfix, checking balanced parentheses, backtracking algorithms (maze solving).

tenMarkQuestions.question: Explain stack with array and linked implementations, operations, and applications.
tenMarkQuestions.answer:
A stack follows LIFO principle with operations at one end (top). 

Array Implementation: Fixed capacity array, top index initialized to -1. Push increments top and stores element. Pop removes from top and decrements top. Peek returns top element. Overflow if top = capacity-1. Underflow if top = -1. Time: O(1) for all operations.

Linked Implementation: Each node has data and next. Head pointer always points to top. Push creates new node, sets next to current head, updates head. Pop moves head to next node. Dynamic size, no overflow condition.

Applications:
1. Browser back button - each visited page is pushed, popping returns to previous.
2. Undo/redo - each action pushed, undo pops last action.
3. Function call stack - each function call pushes frame, returns pop frame.
4. Expression evaluation - postfix evaluation uses stack.
5. Balanced parentheses checking.
6. Backtracking (maze, puzzles).

Conversion: Infix to postfix uses stack to reorder operators based on precedence.

Complexity: All stack operations O(1). Space: O(n) for n elements.
